title: Fans share memories of rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston

input.summary: Hundreds of fans went to Robin Park Arena to sign a book of condolence for the Wigan Warriors star
input.evidence_text: Fans share memories of rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston - BBC News Image caption, Hundreds of fans have paid tribute to Sir Billy Boston by signing the book of condolence at Robin Park Arena By Yunus Mulla Reporting from Wigan Published 1 hour ago Fans have shared memories of the much-loved rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston and signed a book of condolence at his former club Wigan Warriors. Rugby league's first knight died earlier this week aged 92 surrounded by his closest family, the club said. As well as his achievements on the pitch - including scoring 571 tries in his career - a total surpassed only by Australian legend Brian Bevan in top-class rugby league - Boston has a legion of fans heartbroken at the legend's death. The club's kitman, and a lifelong fan who first saw him as a child, and decades later worked for him in his pub when he retired, were among hundreds who went to Robin Park Arena to pay tribute to the star. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Billy Boston who was rugby league's first knight died on Tuesday aged 92 Josie Andrews held back the tears as she told BBC North West Tonight : "I fell in love with Billy Boston when I was eight. "My dad took me to watch him and that is when I fell in love with Wigan rugby." She said she later worked for Boston when he ran the Griffin Hotel close to Wigan's Central Park Ground after he retired from the game. Image caption, Josie Andrews fought back tears as she described how she fell in love with him when her dad took her to watch him at eight Another fan paying his respects was David Mullen who said he met the great man twice and described him as an "absolute gent". "At the ground we always saw Sir Billy and what an absolute guy he was." Image caption, David Mullen Standard bearer for Royal British Leg

In an email sent to George House Trust users and seen by the BBC, the Manchester-based organisation said the material had been downloaded by hackers but not published. The breach is part of a wider cyber security incident potentially affecting up to 1,500 charities across the UK. George House Trust said it was investigating and "taking all appropriate steps". The charity, which was set up in 1985, provides support, advice and information to thousands of people living with HIV. It is unclear how many people connected to the trust have been affected by the breach. The email said personal information including addresses, emails, telephone numbers and "notes and records" about users engagement with the charity was on the database that was targeted. However, it said there was "no sign that any of the data or information" had been "misused in any way at this time". Review carried out The security incident involves technology company Beacon, which operates a database system used by more than a thousand charities across the country. Beacon said the data breach happened at the end of July and it "immediately engaged external cyber security experts to help contain the incident and investigate". The company said it was supporting all the organisations affected. input.summary: Dove Stone reservoir has reopened after firefighters spent more than three weeks tackling a wildfire
input.evidence_text: Dove Stone residents fear parking 'nightmare' after beauty spot reopens - BBC News Image source, Local Democracy Reporting Service Image caption, The beauty spot has been plagued by parking problems, such as here in April 2026 By Ed Barnes , Local Democracy Reporting Service and Haider Saleem , North West , Reporting from North West Published 26 August 2026 People living near a Greater Manchester beauty spot fear a return to a "nightmare" of car-jammed roads and litter after the area reopened following a wildfire. Dove Stone reservoir, near Greenfield in Oldham reopened last week after the blaze burned for more than three weeks. Residents said the area had previously been plagued by obstructed roads, while visitors also left litter and lit barbecues, raising concerns about access for emergency vehicles - and now they fear a return of the same issues. Oldham Council said wardens patrolled the area and issued 946 penalty charge notices around the reservoir in 2025. The RSPB, which manages the attraction's car park, said it understood the concerns. The wildfire began on 11 July and was declared a major incident, with people told to avoid the area while firefighters tackled the blaze. The incident was stood down on 3 August, although crews remained at the scene for days afterwards. Image source, Local Democracy Reporting Service Image caption, Visitors are being urged to respect the landscape and take their litter home Karen O'Connor, who has lived near the reservoir for 35 years, said increasing visitor numbers had made conditions worse - and she worried about emergency access. title: Greater Manchester Police says drones are 'future of policing'

input.lead: A drone unit at Greater Manchester Police is regularly following and helping to catch criminals
input.summary: A drone unit at Greater Manchester Police is regularly following and helping to catch criminals
input.evidence_text: Greater Manchester Police says drones are 'future of policing' - BBC News Image source, Greater Manchester Police Image caption, Police have been using drones to track down bike thieves across the north of Manchester By Richard Stead North West Published 26 August 2026 Drones have been described a "the future of policing" after they were used to help seize 130 illegal off-road bikes across north Manchester in the less than a year. The fleet of drones is being used by Greater Manchester Police instead of the force helicopter because drones are cheaper to use and more discreet. Insp Dan Pickavance, from GMP's North Manchester Neighbourhood Policing Team, said: "All police forces can use drones - particularly in urban areas - and it means we can safely take illegal off-road bikes off the streets. "Using drones is without doubt the future of neighbourhood policing and this is an essential game-changer for us going forward." Image caption, Dan Pickavance, a neighbourhood police inspector for North Manchester, was able to monitor the images from the drone The BBC followed a police operation in which a drone was used to recover a stolen bike that had been spotted in Boggart Hole Clough. The drone was used to follow the bike to an address in nearby Charlestown, where police officers on the ground searched the property and arrested three suspects. The operation was directed by a senior police officer in the back of a van, using live images from the drone which were relayed onto a screen.
